officialTitle: Generative UI for users, not just for designers

chapters.title: The promise of generative UI and the designer–user gap
How a generative UI system works
Envisioning and articulating what you need
Three approaches: prompts, subtasks and surveys
The study: generating and using interfaces
Findings: usability, alignment and prior experience
What the findings mean for task-oriented users
Takeaways: help users envision without designing

existingSummary: Joongi Shin examines generative UI from the perspective of people trying to complete everyday tasks. He compares prompt-only, subtask–UI and prompt-survey approaches in a user study, exploring how design experience, the generation process and follow-up questions affect the resulting experience.

cues.text: So my name is Joongi Shin.
I'm a postdoctoral researcher in Aalto University.
My background is human-computer interaction.
And I'm very fascinated about how emerging technologies help people create something,
but also use something. And I'm here to talk about the generative UI for users,
not just for designers.
So first of all, I would like everyone to get on to this a bit.
Imagine that you are actually planning a three-day winter vacation in Finland.
How would you do it? What kind of interfaces will you go about?
I'll let you think of it.
Probably everyone will try to look for some information about what kind of
activities exist online.
They also go through a list from some blog posts, look at some geographic locations
and also try to make some itineraries.
And some people, you might also have your own particular ways of planning.
Maybe you want to explore these winter activities more systematically, requiring
you to position everything in this kind of plot, and when you click the plot, then it
also shows this kind of further information about the action options.
And wouldn't it be amazing if you can get a functional UI for your task on
demand? And the generative UI is something that enables creating and using functional
interfaces on demand, and this is something I'm going to talk about mainly
today. But I would like you to think about this not as a software developer or
engineers, but from the user who are actually using this interaction
techniques.
So generative UI is promising a future where anyone can create their own
interface. So this is the paper published in a very recent year from Google.
So what they say is that the users who use generative UI, they actually do not need
the design literacy.
They don't really need to understand what is a good design, bad design.
They don't really need to do coding by themselves.
They just need to describe what they want, what kind of task they need to try to do
in natural language.
And then some extreme case, the paper and their work, they also demonstrate just by
saying history of timekeeping devices to LLM, and then the LLM generate this
interactive interface.
So they actually show that this is actually working.
As a researcher, what I'm interested in is, they say anyone, and of course I'm
curious, really anyone can do this.
Despite this, a generative UI technology can be really helpful for any other people
for their daily life, not just for designers or engineers.
When we look at this, how it has been studied is mainly focused on the assisting
designers or from designers' perspective.
For example, this paper looks into how generative UI techniques can be used
across the phase of design practitioners, how they practice design.
And they even find that even for designers, they face a lot of issues when
they try to go about this generative UI interaction.
They also have to think about what kind of design they want to create, what kind of
users needs they need to integrate into their interfaces, and how do you validate
even if AI generates this interactive interface.
And then some interaction approaches actually has been studied quite a bit to
also help design UIs much better.
So after you describe something in a prompt, it's mostly a high-level
description. I want certain interfaces to do certain tasks like planning something,
exploring something, and then that is not really tied to actual interface design in
the end. So what this kind of interaction techniques or process are designed for is
that they try to decompose the prompt into particular UI design specifications so
that designers does not have to iteratively re-describe everything, but
edit particular specifications so they can create the interface that's much more
aligned with what they intended in the beginning.
And then what we want to focus on in this study is that, actually, task-oriented
users is not the same as designers.
Task-oriented users, they just want to perform their task.
Their goal is not to design some beautiful UI.
They are not really familiar with the interactive design practice.
So this actually brings some gap between what, as a user, what is their goal they
want to achieve, compared to designer, whose main intentional motivation is to
actually design the better UIs.
So the research question, in summary, what we explored here is how different
generative UI approaches support task-oriented users in generating and
using UIs. But before I go further into my study, I want to just briefly describe how
the generative UI works.
So a lot of materials are from this paper, the original paper.
And this is the high-level system overview.
And I assume that everyone can recognize very obvious things.
But the author says that there's three most important components.
The first one is the tools, something you can think of it as a server exposing
several end points so that LLMs can actually do some image searches or find
information online, create databases, and so on.
The second one is some system instruction.
This is something probably many of you have known as a system prompt.
I really suggest reading this paper, and then you can find this very, very, very
exhaustive, lengthy descriptions of it.
And then also describe this like what is the design philosophy of generative UI,
how the interface should be created.
Not just like telling AI or yelling at it, why aren't you creating it enough?
And then in a way, it boils down to these four main components in the system
prompt. It gives the goal, what is the goal of the the generating UIs, how the
LLM should plan and think, some example for in-context learning, and some really
massive sets of like a technique instructions.
And then the third component is the post processor that actually tried to fix the
errors that the HTML, CSS, or JavaScript code that LLM generates.
And this is the one that's, for example, replacing fake API keys placeholder to
real API keys, or fixing some bugs and errors.
So this is the high-level conception system overview of the generative UI.
But what I missed is this, like, how is it actually from the user's perspective?
Someone actually will be describing the prompt.
As a researcher, we always look into what kind of theories exist and what is
underlying mechanism that enables people to prompt.
And one of the most recent and also promising theory is the Gulf of
Envisioning, that for people to describe certain their intention on what they want
to achieve by interacting with LLMs, that actually is challenging, very cognitively
challenging task. First of all, you have to know what do you want, right?
You cannot just like tell AI to just create interface, I don't know, that
wouldn't work. It will generate something, but of course, it wouldn't match with what
you were thinking. And the second one is that you also have some expertise in
articulating what you are envisioning.
So imagine that you have this very magical, amazing interfaces that you want
to achieve. It's just sitting in your head, but you don't really know how to
describe it in a particular prompts.
Or you don't know how to effectively describe it so the LLM can generate
something much more aligned with what you wanted it.
So these two are the main gulfs that exist.
And that is actually the reason why we study and design this kind of different
interaction approaches so that people can design something better by exploring what
they really wanted and also align it toward the end goal of what they were
generating from AI lab.
And then coming back to our study, so we compared the three conventional generative
UI approaches. We selected this particular so they represent the particular ways that
has been very easily reachable to any other users.
But first of all, we asked this kind of research questions.
So among these approaches, how does it actually affect users in generating UIs?
How much workload they experience?
How much usability they perceive?
How much they perceive that the final UI is aligned with what they intended?
And what's more importantly, we studied this in the four phases of generating the
UI and having users to use the UIs to complete the given tasks.
The second one is how do users actually experience the generating UI related to
their experience of using UIs.
And the last one is how does this user's prior experiences to generate the UI or
UI/UX design actually affects this overall process.
I'm going to describe a bit more about why we studied these particular things.
First one, what we called as a prompt only as the most like a baseline approach is
that generating UI by just simply conversing with LLM.
And I believe everyone has some experience of like just simply prompting LLMs to
generate some code or interfaces like this, right?
Yeah, so this is anyone can reach this.
The second one is the something that has been studied and very well known to very
useful for designers, generating UI by editing intermediate representations.
So This is not that I'm just prompting something and just working on the final
UI. There is this kind of intermediate representation between the prompt and the
final UI. So as I showed the earlier example, this is as if like a prompt is
composed into the particular UI design element.
And then that is further edited to generate the final UIs.
And in our study, we built on the cognitive walkthrough theory that when
people try to learn new UIs, they actually have some particular processes.
They try to decompose their task into subtask in a certain hierarchical format.
They try to understand what kind of actions are available in the generated UIs
or any UIs that it's facing.
And then they try to map their each subtask and the available actions.
And then they have their own evaluation criteria to understand which mapping works
the best.
So knowing that theory, We assume that this kind of like having decomposing
prompt into a subtask and UI pairs, what could be very easy to understand
representation and something that users can further edit without really learning
about these technologies.
The third one is the generating UI by answering the LLM’s inquiry.
This is something that you can also find some recent updates in the Claude or
ChatGPT, whenever you ask it to do something, it would further ask you some
questions to understand what you really intended for.
So the survey approach is also very promising.
It just generates what LLMs want to ask you and also gives some particular answers
that it is expecting what the answer would be.
So to test this systematically, so we created this interface where on the left
side, this particular interaction is shown, and on the right side, the
generated UI is displayed, so users can actually interact with it and perform the
task they were assigned to during our experiment.
And this is how each approach was looks like.
A bit of the experiment design before I go into the result.
So we test the participants experience in both generating and using UI.
That is the most, one of the very novelty in this study compared to the other prior
work that was focusing only the generation part of it.
They didn't really look into how users will actually use or how designers would
further evaluate what the generated UI would be.
We had 30 participants, and then we intentionally recruited the ones that have
some experience with or without prior generated UI experiences, so we can also
compare the -- analyze the impact of the prior experience.
And then these are the tasks that we gave them.
So three tasks in a randomized order with a different pairing of each approach.
So as you can see, this is a very generic daily task.
You don't really need expertise, so we were really trying to look into whether
this is actually feasibly experienced by generative UI.
So the first findings we made is that the subtask–UI approach felt least usable for
users and the prompt only felt least aligned.
This actually surprising finding for us because a lot of people find the prompt
only approach It's very straightforward and easy to use, and our assumption was
that if you can use it easily, shouldn't it help you align or express your
ideas much better? Also, subtask–UI failing was also surprising because that
was the interaction technique that has been shown to be very working well for
designers. Second finding is that the impressions formed in UI generation were
very strongly associated with the UI use, so if the participants experience any kind
of high effort, they also perceive that using the final generated UI was very
effortful use, despite the quality of UI was not that different between the
participants. The third last one is that the prior experience actually affected
using generated UI. Something interesting finding we observed is that if someone has
an experience in the UI/UX design, they actually perceive less task load when they
are interacting with trying to generate UIs in the prompt-only approach.
This kind of aligns with the prior finding is that if you have much more expertise,
then you know what you can actually describe or what you actually want.
So probably our assumption is that that's why this prompt-only approach felt less
effortful for the ones with some experience.
The one on the right side is showing that prior experience in generative UI for
functioning UI actually have some more even
similar behaviors across the approaches.
So if you have an experience, then you tend to perceive that using the generated
UI is much, much more usable.
We don't have a very clear answer to this, but our assumption was that because you
know what it is, how much you can expect from the LLMs to to generate how much
quality of interfaces can be generated, people, maybe they might have some
different, maybe lower level of expectation compared to the ones who does
not have experience.
So in the end, what does this all mean to us?
I think the first insight I can share is that what works for designers may not
really work for task-oriented users.
So we need to understand what's the difference between designers or engineers
whose task is or goal is to design something better, who are willing and
motivated to iteratively work on it, compared to users who just want to get
something and get their task done.
Second insight is the user needs help envisioning without being made to design.
I think this is a very challenging problem to solve.
So users, of course, they need some help in envisioning because they are not the UI
design experts or engineers of how things work or what is the better things that
they can achieve. However, they also do not want to eat like in a very low level
interact with this kind of intermediate elements.
So in a way prompt only approach was helpful for them so they can just easily
interact with, but there was no assistance at all because they just have to describe
everything. So I think we still need to find a way that we can provide this kind
of interaction. And The last one is the prompt survey approach worked, and we
believe that this is because it helped envision and reduce articulation effort.
So we made this interpretation based on the Gulf of Envisioning earlier as I
described how people need some assistance and how it's actually cognitively
effortful. In the prompt survey approach, LLM pretty much did most of the work,
thinking about, oh, do you actually need this?
What do you mean by you need better interfaces?
So people do not really need to see everything a bit -- every bit by
themselves. Couple of slides to the end.
How do we then move forward to achieve the future that generative UI was aiming for?
Then would be the question that the prompt survey approach is the answer, is the
problem solved? I would say the prompt-survey approach can also fail.
This is also what we observed in our study.
So sometimes LLM just continuously ask questions like that doesn't really align
with or make sense in the human level or what the user was actually wanting to
achieve. For example, they often intentionally ask very obscure, vague
things just to see something up front and then decide based on it.
But still in this kind of survey-based approach, LLM will constantly ask like,
oh, do you actually mean this?
Just to have them to concretely define the ideas.
And also, there could be the case that LLM does not really-- what LLM asks doesn't
really make sense to the people, despite it is still the part of LLM's approach to
try to understand what this person actually means.
So I think the remaining homework for us is that we still need to figure out how
generative UI systems can correctly infer user intention from this kind of vague
prompt without needing people to describe everything.
There are very interesting interaction approaches that has been working on this
field, but I will not go into that detail, but please feel free to reach me out to
discuss this more.
So as a closing, I would like to make this three point as a takeaway.
Generative UI has potential to benefit everyday users beyond designers.
And what works for designers may not work for users.
So I think if you're interested in studying this field, I really want to
strongly suggest that try to differentiate what is the goal the target users or the
target designers that you are aiming for.
And the generative UI should help users envision what they need without making
them design. Thank you.
